correctness.rationale: At a dual vertex the tight-edge graph must be connected: a disconnected component permits a signed slack perturbation after recentering, whereas tight increments determine a connected potential modulo constants. With an A-range of t, feasible B-values lie in [t−1,1] and only the respective extreme levels can have tight incidences; the other split is its transpose. Otherwise same-part differences along tight cross paths are even integers of modulus less than 2, giving just the constant-on-part pair. Centering the split potentials subtracts S²/(2m) from the sum of squares tS−m(t−1); completing the square gives (4). For odd m the profile ((m−1)/2,(m+1)/2) gives error t−1; for even m the central profile gives error zero. Hence split maximizers strictly exceed the constant-on-part normals. Opposite maximal-length normals bound any ball radius, and equality for the centered ball occurs exactly on the maximizing facets. The proof's phrase 'attains equality for every facet' should be read as attaining the upper bound and satisfying every constraint, with tightness only at these facets; the contact formula uses the correct criterion. Optimal centers lie in the common orthogonal complement of the contact normals, and finite strict slack ensures a neighborhood of zero in that complement. Transposition and within-part swaps span both within-part zero-sum spaces. The remaining contrast component is absent exactly in the stated even central-profile case; equal part means in odd size would give error at least t rather than at most t−1. The arithmetic examples, including 88 versus 72 contacts, follow from the indicated profiles.
